questions.q: What does "policy as code" mean, architecturally?
options: Governance rules written as versioned, testable files and applied programmatically, instead of settings clicked in a console
A rule that can only ever be enforced by a human reviewer
A specific Microsoft product with no equivalent elsewhere
Encrypting policy documents so no one can read them
questions.explain: The core idea is that the rule becomes a file with its own version history, the same way application code already works.

questions.q: In an Azure Policy JSON definition, what two parts does the policyRule pair together?
options: An "if" condition and a "then" effect (such as deny, audit, or append)
A username and a password
A start date and an end date
A table name and a column name only
questions.explain: The lesson's verified example shows policyRule built from an if condition and a then.effect, such as deny.

questions.q: What makes Open Policy Agent (OPA) different from a cloud vendor's own built-in policy service?
options: OPA is vendor-neutral and evaluates Rego policies against any JSON input, which is why it shows up across cloud, Kubernetes, and CI/CD alike
OPA can only be used inside one specific cloud provider
OPA requires no policy language at all
OPA only works with row-level security, never other policy types
questions.explain: The lesson describes OPA as a general-purpose engine not tied to one vendor's product, evaluating Rego rules against arbitrary JSON.

questions.q: Why does expressing governance rules as code enable CI/CD-style discipline?
options: Because a text file can go through pull-request review, automated testing, and version-control rollback, the same way application code already does
Because code files are always smaller than console settings
Because CI/CD pipelines cannot run any kind of test on configuration settings
Because policy as code eliminates the need for any review process
questions.explain: The lesson's central CI/CD argument is that a versioned file can be reviewed, tested, and rolled back exactly like application code.

questions.q: According to the lesson, when is policy as code more overhead than it's worth?
options: For a small organization with only a handful of resources and occasional changes
For any organization with more than ten employees
Policy as code is always worth it, with no exceptions
Only when using Open Policy Agent specifically, never Azure Policy
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames policy as code as overkill for a small team with few resources, and increasingly necessary as the number of policies and resources grows.
